title: PhD in Ireland: €31,000 Scholarships, 24-Month Stayback and How Funding Really Works
seoDescription: Ireland PhD funding explained: Government of Ireland scholarships worth €31,000/year, non-EU fees, and the 24-month Third Level Graduate stayback for doctoral graduates.
intro: Ireland pairs flagship €31,000 doctoral scholarships with a 24-month post-study work permit. How the funding system really works and how to stack it.
description: PhD in Ireland: Government of Ireland scholarships, fees, and the 24-month stayback explained for international students.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: Ireland: €31,000 doctoral scholarships and a 24-month stayback — how the funding system really works.
content:
Ireland sells itself as the English-speaking gateway to the EU — and for doctoral researchers, the pitch has substance: four years of funded PhD, a 24-month post-study work permit, and a jobs market where every major tech and pharma company’s European headquarters sits within commuting distance of two research universities. The catch is that Irish doctoral funding is thinner on the ground than in salaried systems, so the funding strategy matters more than the university choice.

How PhD funding actually works in Ireland

Ireland has no salaried-PhD model. Doctoral candidates pay fees (non-EU fees run roughly €12,000-15,000 a year in science and engineering) and fund living costs through scholarships, project grants or their own resources. The flagship national award is the Government of Ireland Postgraduate Scholarship, run by Taighde Éireann (Research Ireland, the merged Irish Research Council and SFI): up to €31,000 a year, structured as a €22,000 stipend, €5,750 towards fees — including non-EU fees — and €3,250 in research expenses. Success rates sit near 18 per cent, calls open in late August and close in early October, with results the following April.

[[chart:ireland-goipg]]
The Irish funding stackWhat it pays

University studentshipsFees + stipend packages, set per project
SFI research centresCohort-based funded PhDs in national research centres
Marie Curie MSCA networksFull package - salary, mobility and family allowances
Industry co-funded PhDsCompany part-funds the studentship; unusually common in Irish pharma and tech

Alongside the national scheme, universities run their own studentships, SFI research centres fund cohort-based PhDs, and European structures — Marie Curie doctoral networks and Ireland-hosted Erasmus Mundus programmes — pay full packages. A realistic Irish plan stacks two or three of these rather than betting everything on one call.

The 24-month stayback

Ireland’s Third Level Graduate Scheme (Stamp 1G) gives non-EU master’s and PhD graduates 24 months to stay and work after finishing — the longest stayback in the English-speaking world after Canada. During those two years you can work full time, switch employers freely, and convert to a general employment permit when a job offers qualifying salary; time served counts towards long-term residence. For doctoral families, spouses on Stamp 1G may also work — a detail that changes household economics considerably.

Where the research jobs actually are

Ireland’s doctoral employment story is unusually concentrated: pharma and biopharma (nearly every major player runs manufacturing or R&D here), medtech, and the data-and-AI operations of the large US technology firms. Doctorates in immunology, process chemistry, data engineering and AI safety feed directly into that pipeline, and industry co-funded PhDs — where a company part-funds the studentship — are more common in Ireland than anywhere else in Europe.

What the years actually cost

Dublin drives every Irish budget conversation. A room in a shared house runs €700-1,000 a month and landlord demand outstrips supply in every term cycle; university accommodation exists but is balloted, not guaranteed. A single funded student — the €22,000 stipend, Dublin rents, modest everything else — lives carefully but legitimately; outside Dublin (Maynooth, Limerick, Galway, Cork), the same stipend behaves like a comfortable wage. Fees are the other half of the arithmetic: non-EU doctoral fees of €12,000-15,000 a year are covered by the national scholarship’s €5,750 contribution only partially, which is why project-funded studentships (fees plus stipend) and co-funded industry places consistently beat self-funded routes on total cost.

Family applicants should model two incomes from the start: Stamp 1G spouses may work without restriction, and Ireland’s employment market for partners is stronger than anywhere else in this guide’s country list — frequently the decisive factor in families choosing Dublin over continental options.

Building a fundable application

  • Start with the supervisor and the centre. Irish awards need a named supervisor’s commitment; SFI research centres (pharma, AI, dairy, marine) run annual funded calls with them.
  • Write the GOI-Postgrad proposal to the rubric. The 18 per cent success rate hides a rubric-driven review: track record, feasibility, and career plan carry explicit weights. Our proposal structure guide maps to it closely.
  • Duplicate across schemes. Run the national call, a centre studentship and a European network application in the same season — the documents overlap by 80 per cent. The EMJM calendar slots the European piece in.
  • Budget year one honestly. Fees hit before any scholarship pays out; confirm payment timing, not just amounts, with your programme.

The live Irish listings below — Tyndall’s funded PhD, University College Cork vacancies and a Maynooth postdoc — are where the stacking strategy starts.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the Government of Ireland Postgraduate Scholarship?

The Government of Ireland Postgraduate Fellowship (IRC/Taighde Éireann) provides a stipend of €25,000 per year (rising where indicated by annual calls), plus €2,250 per year for research expenses and, where eligible, fee contributions. University-based structured PhD programmes typically pay research assistants €19,000-22,000, while SFI/Research Ireland-funded centres pay €22,000-28,000, with living-adjustment top-ups in Dublin.

What is the Third Level Graduate Scheme stayback?

Ireland's Third Level Graduate Scheme grants Master's and PhD graduates a stay-back permission of 24 months to find work — one of Europe's longest. A PhD graduate can additionally move onto an employment permit pathway with reduced salary thresholds, and critical-skills occupation list roles offer a fast route to residency after two years.

Can international students work during an Irish PhD?

Yes — Stamp 2/2A student permission allows up to 20 hours per week during term and 40 hours in scheduled holidays, though doctoral supervisors expect research to remain full-time. Most funded PhD students instead rely on their stipend plus teaching demonstrator hours paid at €20-30 per hour, which universities cap to protect completion times.
